node.description: A British historian of popular politics who met the linguistic turn by combining it with social evidence. With Miles Taylor he replied to Mayfield and Thorne on Stedman Jones (1993) and set out to 'examine critically "electoral sociology"' (1997, as quoted by LoPatin). Speaking for the People (1998) questioned 'the rise of class politics' and 'the triumph of party': the homogenisation thesis of Hobsbawm and of Savage and Miles is examined because 'it remains central to the whole notion of "the rise of class"'; place and gender count for more. Vernon found the book written 'as though … by a schizophrenic'; Lawrence answered, in a response posted in 2010, that 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches must be combined and that scepticism about social data is 'a counsel of despair'. In 2011 he argued that paternalism and 'corporate' identities made Britain's a 'conservative' rather than 'liberal' modernity. Re-reading the Affluent Worker and Bethnal Green interviews (2013–16), he found status and aspiration stronger than the surveys allowed and a 'traditional working class' invented; Me, Me, Me? (2019) holds that community changed, not vanished.

incident_edges.relationship: Speaking for the People's attempt to combine 'material context with discursive representation' is 'ambitious, but ultimately flawed' and reads 'as though it has been written by a schizophrenic'; census and survey data are treated as unproblematic (1999)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Reviews in History 69 (read in full): the book attempts 'a new methodology that combines material context with discursive representation'; it is 'ambitious, but ultimately flawed', treating class and locality as material realities in some chapters and discursive constructs in others; Lawrence treats census and survey data as unproblematic, ignoring how such sources helped constitute the social domain; the book 'singularly fails to move from the local to the national'. incident_edges.relationship: The linguistic turn accepted only in combination: 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches must be combined, and scepticism about social data is 'a counsel of despair' (response posted 2010); the 'retreat from social explanation has by no means been as comprehensive as commentators sometimes suggest' (1998)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own words: response to Vernon (Reviews in History, 1 March 2010, read in full): he is not proposing a new model based on locality; combining 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches is necessary; Vernon's scepticism about social data is 'a counsel of despair'; census data were used for specific questions, not to define class. Ch. 3 opening of Speaking for the People (p. 41, read): 'the retreat from social explanation has by no means been as comprehensive as commentators sometimes suggest'; a 'self-consciously "revisionist" history which retains significant elements of the older historical paradigms'. Vernon's charge of 'schizophrenia' (1999) is the occasion. A critique of the linguistic turn's treatment of social evidence, from one who accepts its questions.

named_group_routes.relationship: The Laurentian narrative: the St. Lawrence commercial system as the basis of a transcontinental Canada (1937), carried through Dominion of the North (1944) and the Macdonald biography (1952–55)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period, his own text. Dominion of the North (1944; pages read in an open copy): the post at Quebec gave the French 'the one great river system which led to the Atlantic seaboard from the heart of the continent'; 'Inevitably the river came to seem the natural basis of a great commercial empire stretching far into the distant west; and the achievement of this empire became the common objective of successive generations of Canadians, though their methods altered and the staple products of their trade were sometimes changed. The first staple of the St. Lawrence commercial system was beaver fur' (p. 21); the rivalry of 'the northern and southern routes, between Montreal and New York, for the control of the Great Lakes system and the command of the western trade', a conflict that 'was to remain essentially the same' (pp. 24–25); 'Quebec had been the origin of the empire of the St. Lawrence; it was to be the genesis of the Dominion of Canada' (p. 298). In-period reception. Herbert Heaton's review (CJEPS, 1938; first page, p. 565, read) quotes the book as 'an attempt to trace the relations between the commercial system of the St. Lawrence and the political development of Canada' (the book's words as Heaton quotes them; the 1937 book is unread) and reads it as a test of the economic interpretation of history that 'has pleased neither the Marxians nor their enemies'. Michel Brunet (RHAF, 1953, p. 579) calls him 'l'un des maîtres contemporains de l'historiographie anglo-canadienne'; Guy Frégault (RHAF, 1955, p. 446) sums up the Macdonald biography as 'Nationalisme antiaméricain, impérialisme et centralisation : synthèse canadienne, — je veux dire anglo-canadienne'. His own retrospect, 1969 (read in full; a later statement by the author, not evidence of what the 1937 book says): 'This Laurentian theme has its basis in the fact that the St. Lawrence is the one great river system that leads from the Atlantic Seaboard to the heart of the continent of North America'; the river 'has inspired generations of Canadians to build a great territorial empire, both commercial and political, in the western interior of the continent' (p. 16); 'The west, it was believed, would make Canada a nation, and the east-west axis would be its backbone' (p. 17); in choosing Macdonald he had 'stumbled upon the only satisfactory method of writing the second phase', so that he had written 'a trilogy on one theme' (p. 16). The phrase, he says, came to be regarded 'as the inspiration, at least in part, of a new school of Canadian historians and as the genesis of a new historical doctrine, the Laurentian interpretation of Canadian history'; he had 'no wish to disavow the parentage of an idea' (p. 14). Later readings: Ouellet (1984, pp. 226–227) calls him 'le chef de l'Ecole laurentienne'; Salmon (1997) says he 'simplified and expanded Innis' thesis'. Contested in period: Brunet found French-Canadian newspapers unread ('Il n'a pas jugé nécessaire de dépouiller un seul journal canadien-français', p. 580) and 'nombreux préjugés' (p. 581); Frégault asked 'où sont les Canadiens français dans tout cela ? Tout simplement, ils n'y sont pas' (p. 447), while praising the work as 'fondé sur une compréhension exacte de l'histoire du Canada' (p. 444); W. L. Morton, as quoted by Davis (1985), saw in Creighton 'the preponderant role commercial monopoly and centralized business have played' (Davis, p. 97) and held that the metropolitan thesis, which he associated with Creighton and Careless, 'seems necessarily to minimize the importance of the hinterland' (Davis, p. 98); the critic George Woodcock (1979, p. 140) called his treatment of Confederation as centralist 'a major distortion'. A contribution, not a founding.

named_group_routes.relationship: Innis's staple studies as a resource for Creighton's Laurentian narrative, as Creighton's own staple vocabulary and later readers show; Creighton rejected the story that the 1937 book grew from their friendship
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own texts. Dominion of the North (1944) frames the St. Lawrence system by its staples ('The first staple of the St. Lawrence commercial system was beaver fur', p. 21), and its reading list (pp. 505–507) names Innis's The Fur Trade in Canada (1930) and The Cod Fisheries (1940). The 1957 presidential address recalls 'the 1930's, when the influence of Harold Innis was at its height and everybody was writing and talking about staple production' (p. 3), and exempts Innis from the Marxian fashion: 'most of the professional economists — and especially Innis — refused to accept the simplified Marxian version of historical determinism' (p. 6). In 1957 he also published Harold Adams Innis: Portrait of a Scholar (unread); Benoît Brouillette's review (1957, p. 529, read) reports Creighton's account of Innis's Canada as an east–west system 'marqué par le Saint-Laurent et les Grands-Lacs', at once 'transocéanique et transcontinental'. The qualification, his own (1969, pp. 14–15): 'The Empire of the St. Lawrence, it is sometimes confidently asserted, was the fruit of my friendship with Harold Innis ... These explanations, like most simple generalizations, happen to be wrong'; the subject was suggested 'not by Harold Innis, whom I barely knew at the time, but by W. P. M. Kennedy', and he was 'reluctantly convinced by the weight of his own evidence' about the Montreal merchants (p. 16). Readers: George Woodcock (1979, p. 134): 'Creighton's master was H. A. Innis, especially the Innis of The Fur Trade in Canada, which contained the essential germ out of which — with Innis's encouragement — Creighton built the scenario of his first book'; Fernand Ouellet (1984, p. 226): Creighton started 'partant de la théorie des staples'; Deborah Harrison (1981), as quoted by Davis (1985, p. 97): 'probably the first to advance a metropolitanist interpretation, although the closely related "staples" thesis had been put forward by Innis much earlier'; Salmon (1997): he 'simplified and expanded Innis' thesis'. The edge records Innis's work as a resource the Laurentian narrative used, not a teacher–pupil derivation; Creighton's denial concerns the origin of the subject, not the use of the staple framework.
named_group_routes.map_label: Staples behind the Laurentian narrative, contested

named_group_routes.relationship: Embodied, sensory histories of megaprojects and environmental change in Canada, 1953–2003 (2006–10)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Dated 2006–2011; no claim here concerns her work before 2000. Sensing Changes: Technologies, Environments, and the Everyday, 1953–2003 (UBC Press, 2010) is unread here. As Jackson quotes it (Senses and Society 6:2, 2011, read in full), Parr seeks to move beyond 'representations . . . in language . . . , to open interpretive space in which to study the robust materiality of technologies, environments, and the everyday, to encounter them as directly and as fleshly as possible' (p. 9). Jackson describes chapters on the NATO base at Gagetown, nuclear power and heavy water on Lake Huron, the St Lawrence Seaway at Iroquois, the Columbia River reservoir and Walkerton's water, each read through a sense ('Smell and Risk', 'Taste and Expertise'). She adds that Parr counts proprioception, kinesthetics and proxemics among the senses (pp. 225–27). Jackson places the book in the UBC Press Nature/History/Culture series (p. 225). Rumiel (Left History 15:1, 2011, read in full) notes 'the people whose lives and senses of self had been transformed' by megaprojects (p. 189). She suggests that 'a comparative analysis of a related case in a Canadian Aboriginal or Inuit community' was a missed opportunity (p. 189). The environmental line begins earlier with 'Smells Like?: Sources of Uncertainty in the History of the Great Lakes Environment' (Environmental History 11:2, 2006; metadata only). A contribution: it records her later field, not influence on environmental history's formation.

named_group_routes.relationship: Creighton's characterisation of post-Conquest French Canada as a decadent feudal society, cited approvingly by Ouellet and Hamelin in the 1962 crisis article
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Ouellet and Hamelin (1962, p. 32, read): the crisis reveals two cultural entities of unequal evolution, 'C'est pourquoi le professeur Creighton a pu parler, en se référant à la société canadienne-française, de société féodale décadente.' Ouellet's own 1984 survey (recorded by the 1.136 Creighton packet, pp. 226–227; not re-read here) summarises Creighton's post-Conquest French Canada as 'une société semi-féodale décadente devenue hostile aux impératifs économiques'. In-period critics pair them: Paquet and Wallot (1972, p. 186 n. 5) cite 'D. G. Creighton, The Empire of the St. Lawrence (2e éd., Toronto, 1956) et F. Ouellet, Histoire économique et sociale du Québec' as the 'historiographie traditionnelle' that saw restructurings but not modernisation; Tousignant (1980, p. 416) says the 1966 book 'faisait écho aux vieux préjugés de l'historiographie canadienne-anglaise' (no historian named). The influence rests on the 1962 citation alone; the critics' pairing and Ouellet's 1984 comparison are context and do not independently establish transmission. The edge records a borrowed characterisation, not a teacher–pupil lineage; Ouellet's Labroussian method has other sources (edge_874; edge 6).

named_group_routes.relationship: A narrative of four charivaris cited by Stone among works turning to narrative, after she criticised his draft (1979); later, pardon tales read as crafted stories without discrediting the archives (1987)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Stone, Past & Present 85 (1979), read: p. 3, starred note, thanks ‘Natalie Davis’ among colleagues ‘for valuable criticism of an early draft of this paper’; p. 18: ‘Natalie Davis has presented a narrative of four charivaris or ritual public shame procedures in seventeenth-century Lyon and Geneva, in order to illustrate community efforts to enforce public standards of honour and propriety’ (n. 29, the essay forthcoming in Le Goff and Schmitt, Le charivari). Her own account (1997, p. 21, read): she called her 1987 book Fiction in the Archives ‘somewhat to the consternation of Lawrence Stone to whom it was dedicated’; ‘“fiction” referred not to falsification, but to the crafting element in everything we do and say. Rather than being on an extreme anti-foundationalist mission to discredit the archives, I was presenting them as a source of new evidence’. As the revival scope requires, being named by Stone does not imply that she accepted his diagnosis. Fiction in the Archives is unread.

named_group_routes.relationship: Hill's revisions of the 'bourgeois revolution' read as the inspiration for Brenner's 'another social interpretation' of the English Revolution (1993)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Wood, 'Christopher Hill and the Recovery of History' (Against the Current, 2003, read in full): 'Other Marxists, notably Robert Brenner, have developed another social interpretation … (See especially the Conclusion to Brenner's Merchants and Revolution …) It hardly needs saying that Hill's pioneering work has inspired these fruitful developments in Marxist historiography.' named_group_routes.relationship: Tilly: 'shrill bravado', 'softcore solipsism' and a dismissal of democratic politics that his own evidence contradicts (1994); Lawrence asked 'The Decline of English Popular Politics?' (1994); Oddy found 'verbose but superficial' method in Hunger (2008); Craig doubted modernity as a singular condition (2016)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Tilly 1994, read in full: 'Joyce fretfully and Vernon with shrill bravado' (p. 260); 'the Joyce-Vernon philosophical position obliterates any possibility of historical explanation' (p. 261); by Tilly's criteria Vernon's own evidence 'establishes a modest but real increase in democracy' (p. 268). Craig (2016, read) doubts modernity as a singular condition. Lawrence's 1994 review is known by its title only. Vernon's own answers are on his entry and on his 2009 response to Oddy.

named_group_routes.relationship: Wilentz's American exceptionalism exchange (1984) and Katznelson's call to return to political history (1994) ran beside the British linguistic turn; Eley and Nield endorsed 'his desire to avoid binarisms' while keeping 'some basic disagreements' (2000)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Editors' remarks, ILWCH 26 (1984, read in full): 'Twenty-some years ago the interests of historians of the working class shifted sharply away from parties and organizational leaders toward the actions, aspirations, and thinking of the working people themselves'; Hanagan: 'The ways in which working-class struggles have been embedded in a county's [sic] political structure do make a difference' (p. v). The British new political history is drawn on the Vernon and Lawrence entries and the strand political/new_political_history. Moderate.

named_group_routes.relationship: The Laurentian narrative: the St. Lawrence commercial system as the basis of a transcontinental Canada (1937), carried through Dominion of the North (1944) and the Macdonald biography (1952–55)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period, his own text. Dominion of the North (1944; pages read in an open copy): the post at Quebec gave the French 'the one great river system which led to the Atlantic seaboard from the heart of the continent'; 'Inevitably the river came to seem the natural basis of a great commercial empire stretching far into the distant west; and the achievement of this empire became the common objective of successive generations of Canadians, though their methods altered and the staple products of their trade were sometimes changed. The first staple of the St. Lawrence commercial system was beaver fur' (p. 21); the rivalry of 'the northern and southern routes, between Montreal and New York, for the control of the Great Lakes system and the command of the western trade', a conflict that 'was to remain essentially the same' (pp. 24–25); 'Quebec had been the origin of the empire of the St. Lawrence; it was to be the genesis of the Dominion of Canada' (p. 298). In-period reception. Herbert Heaton's review (CJEPS, 1938; first page, p. 565, read) quotes the book as 'an attempt to trace the relations between the commercial system of the St. Lawrence and the political development of Canada' (the book's words as Heaton quotes them; the 1937 book is unread) and reads it as a test of the economic interpretation of history that 'has pleased neither the Marxians nor their enemies'. Michel Brunet (RHAF, 1953, p. 579) calls him 'l'un des maîtres contemporains de l'historiographie anglo-canadienne'; Guy Frégault (RHAF, 1955, p. 446) sums up the Macdonald biography as 'Nationalisme antiaméricain, impérialisme et centralisation : synthèse canadienne, — je veux dire anglo-canadienne'. His own retrospect, 1969 (read in full; a later statement by the author, not evidence of what the 1937 book says): 'This Laurentian theme has its basis in the fact that the St. Lawrence is the one great river system that leads from the Atlantic Seaboard to the heart of the continent of North America'; the river 'has inspired generations of Canadians to build a great territorial empire, both commercial and political, in the western interior of the continent' (p. 16); 'The west, it was believed, would make Canada a nation, and the east-west axis would be its backbone' (p. 17); in choosing Macdonald he had 'stumbled upon the only satisfactory method of writing the second phase', so that he had written 'a trilogy on one theme' (p. 16). The phrase, he says, came to be regarded 'as the inspiration, at least in part, of a new school of Canadian historians and as the genesis of a new historical doctrine, the Laurentian interpretation of Canadian history'; he had 'no wish to disavow the parentage of an idea' (p. 14). Later readings: Ouellet (1984, pp. 226–227) calls him 'le chef de l'Ecole laurentienne'; Salmon (1997) says he 'simplified and expanded Innis' thesis'. Contested in period: Brunet found French-Canadian newspapers unread ('Il n'a pas jugé nécessaire de dépouiller un seul journal canadien-français', p. 580) and 'nombreux préjugés' (p. 581); Frégault asked 'où sont les Canadiens français dans tout cela ? Tout simplement, ils n'y sont pas' (p. 447), while praising the work as 'fondé sur une compréhension exacte de l'histoire du Canada' (p. 444); W. L. Morton, as quoted by Davis (1985), saw in Creighton 'the preponderant role commercial monopoly and centralized business have played' (Davis, p. 97) and held that the metropolitan thesis, which he associated with Creighton and Careless, 'seems necessarily to minimize the importance of the hinterland' (Davis, p. 98); the critic George Woodcock (1979, p. 140) called his treatment of Confederation as centralist 'a major distortion'. A contribution, not a founding.

named_group_routes.relationship: Innis's staple studies as a resource for Creighton's Laurentian narrative, as Creighton's own staple vocabulary and later readers show; Creighton rejected the story that the 1937 book grew from their friendship
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own texts. Dominion of the North (1944) frames the St. Lawrence system by its staples ('The first staple of the St. Lawrence commercial system was beaver fur', p. 21), and its reading list (pp. 505–507) names Innis's The Fur Trade in Canada (1930) and The Cod Fisheries (1940). The 1957 presidential address recalls 'the 1930's, when the influence of Harold Innis was at its height and everybody was writing and talking about staple production' (p. 3), and exempts Innis from the Marxian fashion: 'most of the professional economists — and especially Innis — refused to accept the simplified Marxian version of historical determinism' (p. 6). In 1957 he also published Harold Adams Innis: Portrait of a Scholar (unread); Benoît Brouillette's review (1957, p. 529, read) reports Creighton's account of Innis's Canada as an east–west system 'marqué par le Saint-Laurent et les Grands-Lacs', at once 'transocéanique et transcontinental'. The qualification, his own (1969, pp. 14–15): 'The Empire of the St. Lawrence, it is sometimes confidently asserted, was the fruit of my friendship with Harold Innis ... These explanations, like most simple generalizations, happen to be wrong'; the subject was suggested 'not by Harold Innis, whom I barely knew at the time, but by W. P. M. Kennedy', and he was 'reluctantly convinced by the weight of his own evidence' about the Montreal merchants (p. 16). Readers: George Woodcock (1979, p. 134): 'Creighton's master was H. A. Innis, especially the Innis of The Fur Trade in Canada, which contained the essential germ out of which — with Innis's encouragement — Creighton built the scenario of his first book'; Fernand Ouellet (1984, p. 226): Creighton started 'partant de la théorie des staples'; Deborah Harrison (1981), as quoted by Davis (1985, p. 97): 'probably the first to advance a metropolitanist interpretation, although the closely related "staples" thesis had been put forward by Innis much earlier'; Salmon (1997): he 'simplified and expanded Innis' thesis'. The edge records Innis's work as a resource the Laurentian narrative used, not a teacher–pupil derivation; Creighton's denial concerns the origin of the subject, not the use of the staple framework.
named_group_routes.map_label: Staples behind the Laurentian narrative, contested

named_group_routes.relationship: Embodied, sensory histories of megaprojects and environmental change in Canada, 1953–2003 (2006–10)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Dated 2006–2011; no claim here concerns her work before 2000. Sensing Changes: Technologies, Environments, and the Everyday, 1953–2003 (UBC Press, 2010) is unread here. As Jackson quotes it (Senses and Society 6:2, 2011, read in full), Parr seeks to move beyond 'representations . . . in language . . . , to open interpretive space in which to study the robust materiality of technologies, environments, and the everyday, to encounter them as directly and as fleshly as possible' (p. 9). Jackson describes chapters on the NATO base at Gagetown, nuclear power and heavy water on Lake Huron, the St Lawrence Seaway at Iroquois, the Columbia River reservoir and Walkerton's water, each read through a sense ('Smell and Risk', 'Taste and Expertise'). She adds that Parr counts proprioception, kinesthetics and proxemics among the senses (pp. 225–27). Jackson places the book in the UBC Press Nature/History/Culture series (p. 225). Rumiel (Left History 15:1, 2011, read in full) notes 'the people whose lives and senses of self had been transformed' by megaprojects (p. 189). She suggests that 'a comparative analysis of a related case in a Canadian Aboriginal or Inuit community' was a missed opportunity (p. 189). The environmental line begins earlier with 'Smells Like?: Sources of Uncertainty in the History of the Great Lakes Environment' (Environmental History 11:2, 2006; metadata only). A contribution: it records her later field, not influence on environmental history's formation.

named_group_routes.relationship: Creighton's characterisation of post-Conquest French Canada as a decadent feudal society, cited approvingly by Ouellet and Hamelin in the 1962 crisis article
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Ouellet and Hamelin (1962, p. 32, read): the crisis reveals two cultural entities of unequal evolution, 'C'est pourquoi le professeur Creighton a pu parler, en se référant à la société canadienne-française, de société féodale décadente.' Ouellet's own 1984 survey (recorded by the 1.136 Creighton packet, pp. 226–227; not re-read here) summarises Creighton's post-Conquest French Canada as 'une société semi-féodale décadente devenue hostile aux impératifs économiques'. In-period critics pair them: Paquet and Wallot (1972, p. 186 n. 5) cite 'D. G. Creighton, The Empire of the St. Lawrence (2e éd., Toronto, 1956) et F. Ouellet, Histoire économique et sociale du Québec' as the 'historiographie traditionnelle' that saw restructurings but not modernisation; Tousignant (1980, p. 416) says the 1966 book 'faisait écho aux vieux préjugés de l'historiographie canadienne-anglaise' (no historian named). The influence rests on the 1962 citation alone; the critics' pairing and Ouellet's 1984 comparison are context and do not independently establish transmission. The edge records a borrowed characterisation, not a teacher–pupil lineage; Ouellet's Labroussian method has other sources (edge_874; edge 6).

named_group_routes.relationship: A narrative of four charivaris cited by Stone among works turning to narrative, after she criticised his draft (1979); later, pardon tales read as crafted stories without discrediting the archives (1987)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Stone, Past & Present 85 (1979), read: p. 3, starred note, thanks ‘Natalie Davis’ among colleagues ‘for valuable criticism of an early draft of this paper’; p. 18: ‘Natalie Davis has presented a narrative of four charivaris or ritual public shame procedures in seventeenth-century Lyon and Geneva, in order to illustrate community efforts to enforce public standards of honour and propriety’ (n. 29, the essay forthcoming in Le Goff and Schmitt, Le charivari). Her own account (1997, p. 21, read): she called her 1987 book Fiction in the Archives ‘somewhat to the consternation of Lawrence Stone to whom it was dedicated’; ‘“fiction” referred not to falsification, but to the crafting element in everything we do and say. Rather than being on an extreme anti-foundationalist mission to discredit the archives, I was presenting them as a source of new evidence’. As the revival scope requires, being named by Stone does not imply that she accepted his diagnosis. Fiction in the Archives is unread.
